Joint outliers · the word

Concept A joint outlier is ordinary in every column and unusual as a combination.

checkup.csv, the 7 unit errors from lecture 4 corrected
Row 136 is 186.0 cm and 50.5 kg. Tall adults exist and light adults exist; this pair sits far off the trend.

What lecture 4 saw

Every method there looked at one column. The 5 joint rows score 1.35 to 2.57 in absolute z on either column, and none was flagged.

What changes today

Every method measures distance or density in both columns at once, so the trend between them becomes part of the yardstick.

The trend is the information. Height and weight correlate at 0.545 here, and a joint outlier breaks that relationship.
Joint outliers · the five rows

Example Each of the 5 joint rows stays under 2.6 in z on both columns. Their Mahalanobis d² runs 11.5 to 18.4, against a cutoff of 7.38.

checkup.csv · 500 rows

Lecture 4's file with the 3 decimal slips and 4 pound entries corrected. Left: 5 joint rows, 2 real extremes, 493 clean.

shops.csv · 306 rows, generated

150 kiosks packed around 40 sqm, 150 supermarkets spread over 200 to 600 sqm, 2 global outliers and 4 local ones. Built by make_shops.py, seed 2402.

A local outlier is close to the kiosks by the standard of the whole file and far from them by the standard of a kiosk.
Mahalanobis distance

Concept Measure distance from the centre in units of the cloud's own spread and tilt, so the contour is an ellipse.

the 97.5% ellipse on checkup
d² = (x − μ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (x − μ) flag the row when d² > χ²₂(0.975) = 7.378

Mahalanobis, 1936

P. C. Mahalanobis introduced it to compare anthropometric measurements, where every variable moves with every other.

Why an ellipse

Along the trend a large gap is expected. Across it, a small gap is already unusual.

Mahalanobis distance · step 1 of 6

Intuition One column at a time, the squared z is χ² on 1 degree of freedom: the kernel of Little's test and of Grubbs.

row 136, one column at a time
z_height = (186.0 − 166.53) / 9.14 = +2.13 z_weight = (50.5 − 71.03) / 11.48 = -1.79
Height alone: z² = 4.54 > 3.841, a rejection at 5%.
Weight alone: z² = 3.20, inside.
Two tests on one row, and neither knows about the other column.
Mahalanobis distance · step 2 of 6

Intuition continued 1 Add the two squared z's. If the columns were independent the sum would be χ² on 2 df, and the contour a circle.

standardised height and weight, circle at d² = 7.378
d² = z_h² + z_w² = 4.54 + 3.20 = 7.74 cutoff χ²₂(0.975) = 7.378
Row 136 lands just outside the circle.

The circle flags 24 rows

3 joint, 1 real and 20 clean. All 20 clean rows are tall and heavy, or short and light.

Those clean rows sit on the trend. The circle ignores it.
Mahalanobis distance · step 3 of 6

Intuition continued 2 Height and weight correlate at 0.545. Undo the correlation and the circle tilts into an ellipse along the trend.

same data, the ellipse at the same cutoff
d² = (z_h² − 2ρ z_h z_w + z_w²) / (1 − ρ²)
row 136: z_h +2.13, z_w -1.79 circle 7.74 → ellipse 16.91
row 34: z_h +2.01, z_w +1.83 circle 7.38 → ellipse 4.80
Opposite signs push d² up, matching signs pull it down. The cross term charges for going against the trend.
Mahalanobis distance · step 4 of 6

Intuition continued 3 For p columns the same idea is a quadratic form in the inverse covariance, χ² on p df under multivariate normality.

the 97.5% ellipse in the original units
d² = (x − μ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (x − μ) ~ χ²_p μ = (166.53, 71.03) Σ = [[83.5, 57.2], [57.2, 131.9]]
Little's step 6 used this same form on each missingness pattern's mean. Here it runs on one row.

15 rows flagged

All 5 joint rows, both real extremes and 8 clean rows. 2.5% of 500 normal rows is 12.5.

Mahalanobis distance · step 5 of 6

Intuition continued 4 Estimate μ and Σ with lecture 4's 7 unit errors still in the file, and the ellipse swells until the joint rows fit inside.

Every joint row falls under 7.38. So do the 4 pound entries. Only the 3 decimal slips are flagged.
Masking again, now in two dimensions: the outliers inflate the covariance that is used to judge them.
The green ellipse is the minimum covariance determinant (MCD) fit: μ and Σ from the tightest half of the rows. The errors fall outside that half, so the ellipse stays tight. The next slide builds it.
Mahalanobis distance · step 6 of 6

Intuition continued 5 Estimate μ and Σ from the tightest half of the rows only. On the uncorrected file this finds all 14 planted rows.

weight as recorded, with the robust ellipse

Minimum covariance determinant

Rousseeuw, 1984. Search for the h rows, about half, whose covariance has the smallest determinant: the tightest ellipse that holds half the data.

on the uncorrected file: decimal 3/3 pounds 4/4 joint 5/5 real 2/2 clean 16
The robust median of lecture 4 had a breakdown point of 50%. MCD brings the same property to a covariance matrix.
Mahalanobis distance · step 6 of 6 · the search

Intuition continued 6 MCD finds its h rows by C-steps: keep the 251 rows nearest the current ellipse, refit, repeat. From a start holding a pound entry, 10 steps reach det 562.5.

weight as recorded, one random start, one C-step per press

Finding the h rows

h = ⌊(n + p + 1)/2⌋ = 251, for n = 500 rows and p = 2 columns. There are about 10149 subsets of that size. FAST-MCD (Rousseeuw and Van Driessen, 1999) searches from random starts instead, and a C-step cannot raise the determinant.

C-step: score all 500 rows against the current ellipse, keep the 251 smallest d². det Σ planted rows start, 3 rows 52,366 1 pound step 1 1,942 3 pound, 1 real step 2 827 0 steps 3 to 9 703→563 0 step 10 562.5 0, subset unchanged
500 random starts settle between det 562.5 and 570.3, and none of the 500 final subsets holds a planted row. FAST-MCD keeps the smallest.
Mahalanobis distance

Example Row 34 is 184.9 cm and 92.0 kg, about 2 sd up on both columns. d² = 4.80, inside the ellipse.

row 34 sits on the trend
z_h = +2.01 z_w = +1.83 d² = (2.01² − 2·0.545·2.01·1.83 + 1.83²) / (1 − 0.545²) = 4.80 < 7.378

Not flagged

A tall, heavy adult is what the trend predicts. The circle put this row right on its boundary at 7.38.

Mahalanobis distance

Test Row 136 has d² = 16.91 on 2 df, p = 2.1e-04. It is rejected at 2.5%.

row 136 against the ellipse
H₀the row comes from the multivariate normal fitted to the file
H₁it came from another process

decisiond² = 16.91: reject

The multiple-testing bill

500 rows tested at once need 2.5%/500, a cutoff of 19.81. All 5 joint rows fall under it, row 138 at 18.42 included. Only one real extreme is flagged.

The same trade as Grubbs: a stricter cutoff buys fewer false flags and loses real outliers.
Mahalanobis distance

Mahalanobis distance

Assumptions 4 conditions, and the second one is the one shops.csv breaks.

AssumptionWhat happens when it fails
The clean rows are close to multivariate normalThe χ² reference and the elliptical contour both come from it. Skewed columns need a transform first.
One cloudTwo populations in one file get one ellipse that fits neither.
μ and Σ come from clean rowsClassical estimates on the raw checkup file flag none of the 5 joint rows. Use MCD when outliers may be in the file.
Many more rows than columnsΣ must be invertible. With p close to n the estimate is unstable, and MCD needs h > p.
Mahalanobis distance

Drawbacks On shops the classical ellipse flags the 2 global rows and nothing else. The local rows score d² 1.29 to 1.79.

shops with the classical and the MCD ellipse

Classical: too wide

One ellipse stretched over both formats. Every kiosk and every local outlier sits deep inside it.

MCD: too narrow

The tightest half is the kiosks, so MCD flags 156 rows: all 150 supermarkets along with the 6 planted ones.

Any method with one global centre and one global spread fails on two formats. The next method measures density locally.
LOF

Concept Compare each row's local density with the density of its neighbours. A row much sparser than its neighbours is an outlier.

shops: the 4 local and 2 global outliers

Breunig, Kriegel, Ng and Sander, 2000

Local Outlier Factor. A score near 1 means as dense as the neighbourhood; well above 1 means sparser.

Why local

A supermarket 40 sqm from its neighbour is ordinary. A kiosk-sized shop 30 thousand rupees off the kiosks is not.

Six steps build the score, each fixing one problem with the last. All distances are on standardised columns.
LOF · step 1 of 6

Intuition Take the distance to the k-th nearest neighbour. Row 245 needs 0.227 to reach its 10th; a typical kiosk needs far less.

the 10 nearest neighbours of two rows
k-distance(p) = distance from p to its k-th nearest neighbour Nₖ(p) = those k neighbours
Row 245 is 40 sqm and ₹72 thousand, a kiosk's floor with nearly twice a kiosk's sales.
The median kiosk's 10th neighbour is 0.012 away.
Large k-distance, isolated row. That is the kernel of every density method.
LOF · step 2 of 6

Intuition continued 1 Rank all rows by k-distance and the top 14 are 12 supermarkets and the 2 global rows. No local row makes it.

the 14 largest k-distances ringed
plantedmedian k-distance
kiosk0.012
supermarket0.160
local0.167
global1.740
A local row is as far from its neighbours as an ordinary supermarket is from its own.
k-distance is still a global yardstick. The fix is to compare each row with its own neighbours.
LOF · step 3 of 6

Intuition continued 2 Replace each distance to a neighbour by at least that neighbour's own k-distance. Rows deep in a cluster stop looking artificially dense.

reachability distance from p to two neighbours

In words

Inside the kiosk cluster, two rows can sit almost on top of each other. A distance near zero makes 1 ÷ distance enormous, and the density would jump with every tiny gap.

Reachability puts a floor under each distance. The distance from p to a neighbour o counts as at least o's own k-distance, the radius of o's circle. A row inside that circle is treated as sitting on its edge.

An isolated row lies outside its neighbours' circles, so it keeps its full distances. The floor steadies dense clusters and leaves outliers with their long distances.

reach-distₖ(p, o) = max( k-distance(o), d(p, o) )

Inside a neighbour's circle

p is treated as sitting on the circle's edge. Small random gaps between near-duplicates no longer drive the score.

Outside it

The plain distance is kept. An isolated row keeps its large distances.

Reachability is not symmetric: reach-dist(p, o) uses o's k-distance, not p's.
LOF · step 4 of 6

Intuition continued 3 Local reachability density is one over the mean reachability distance to the k neighbours. Row 245 has 4.60.

lrd of row 245's 10 neighbours, then row 245

In words

Local reachability density turns those distances into a crowding score: 1 ÷ the average reachability distance to the k neighbours. Close neighbours give a high density, distant ones a low density.

A median kiosk scores 84.17 and a median supermarket 6.45. Row 245 scores 4.60, close to a supermarket, and a supermarket is ordinary.

The density still needs a reference: the density of row 245's own neighbours. The next step supplies it.

lrdₖ(p) = 1 / mean over o in Nₖ(p) of reach-distₖ(p, o)

global0.61
A local row is about as dense as a supermarket. Density alone still cannot separate them.

LOF · step 5 of 6

Intuition continued 4 Divide the neighbours' mean density by the row's own. Row 245: 27.76 / 4.60 = 6.04.

row 245 against its neighbours, with their mean

In words

Row 245's 10 nearest neighbours are kiosks with a mean lrd of 27.76. Its own lrd is 4.60, so LOF = 27.76 / 4.60 = 6.04: row 245 is six times sparser than the area it sits in.

An ordinary row is about as dense as its neighbours, so its ratio is near 1. A kiosk among kiosks divides one high density by another; a supermarket among supermarkets divides two low ones. Both groups have a median LOF of 1.04.

Mahalanobis measures how far a row is from the centre of the whole file. LOF measures how much sparser a row is than its own neighbours. That is how it catches a shop that is ordinary file-wide and odd among kiosks.

LOFₖ(p) = mean over o in Nₖ(p) of lrd(o) ÷ lrd(p) row 245 = 27.76 / 4.60 = 6.04
plantedmedian LOF
kiosk1.04
supermarket1.04
local6.11
global7.62
Kiosks and supermarkets both sit at 1.04. The two densities cancel in the ratio.
LOF has no p-value, so the cutoff is a choice. The next slides flag rows with LOF above 1.5, a common rule of thumb; the Test slide returns to it.
LOF · step 6 of 6

Intuition continued 5 The score depends on k. All 6 planted rows pass 1.5 at every k from 3 to 50; the clean rows flagged with them change with k.

rows with LOF above 1.5, for k from 3 to 50

In words

k sets the size of the neighbourhood each row is compared with.

At k = 3 each density rests on 3 distances, so chance gaps between a few points decide the score. 33 rows pass 1.5, and the clean ones among them are scattered through both clusters.

At k = 40 the neighbourhood covers a large part of the cluster. Rows on the rim are compared with the dense core and score high: 31 rows pass, and the 25 clean ones sit on the outer edge of their own cluster.

All 6 planted rows pass 1.5 at every k from 3 to 50. The choice of k changes which clean rows are flagged with them.

Small k

Few neighbours, noisy densities. At k = 3 the rule flags 33 rows.

Large k

The neighbourhood covers much of a cluster, and its rim scores high. At k = 40 it flags 31.

Breunig et al. suggest scoring over a range of k and keeping each row's maximum. Here k = 9 gives the fewest flags, 14.

LOF

Test LOF has no null distribution, so the test is a cutoff you choose. At 1.5 it flags 14 rows, the 6 planted ones among them.

Common cutoffs

1.5 and 2 are rules of thumb. The alternative is a count: inspect the top 1% or the top 20.

What the number means

LOF 6 says the row is six times sparser than its neighbourhood. It says nothing about a probability.

Mahalanobis had a χ² reference. From here on, every method hands back a ranking and leaves the cutoff to you.
LOF

Mechanism The score written out whole, with the four local rows worked through it.

Distances are Euclidean on standardised columns. sklearn's LocalOutlierFactor gives the same scores to 8 decimals.

LOF

Assumptions 3 conditions, all about what a neighbourhood means.

AssumptionWhat happens when it fails
Distance means somethingArea in sqm and sales in thousands differ in scale. Unscaled, one column decides every neighbour. Standardise first, and choose which columns count.
k sits between the outlier group and the smallest clusterA group of k or more outliers becomes its own dense neighbourhood and scores near 1.
Few columnsIn high dimension all pairwise distances look alike, and density loses its contrast.
LOF

Drawbacks No probability, a k to choose, and every pairwise distance to compute. Move k and watch which clean rows join the flagged set.

Cost

A naive run compares every pair: 306² here, 10¹² for a million rows. Index structures help only in low dimension.

What k changes

Which clean rows are flagged alongside the planted ones.

Isolation Forest

Concept Cut the data at random until a row stands alone. An outlier stands alone early; this global row took 5 cuts.

one random tree, one cut per press

Liu, Ting and Zhou, 2008

Pick a column at random, then a split value at random between its min and max. Repeat on the side holding the row.

Why it works

A row far from the rest is separated by almost any cut. A row inside a crowd needs many cuts to be peeled away from its neighbours.

No distances and no densities. The method only counts cuts.
Isolation Forest

Example Over 200 trees the median path length is 3.57 cuts for the global rows, 6.78 for the local ones, and 13.45 for kiosks.

one tree isolating a central kiosk: 14 cuts drawn
plantedmedian E(h), cuts
global3.57
local6.78
supermarket11.33
kiosk13.45

Local rows isolate fast too

The kiosks are packed so tightly that a row just beside them is cut away early.

The top 14 scores hold all 6 planted rows, with the same result under 10 different random seeds.
Isolation Forest

Mechanism The average path length is scaled by the expected path in a random tree of the subsample size, c(256) = 10.24, and turned into a score.

the score over the whole plane, 200 trees
s(x) = 2^( −E[h(x)] / c(ψ) ) c(ψ) = 2 H(ψ − 1) − 2(ψ − 1)/ψ ψ = 256 rows per tree, c = 10.24
E(h)s
global3.570.785
local6.780.632
kiosk13.450.403
s near 1: isolated quickly. s at 0.5 or below: an ordinary row. H is the harmonic number.
Isolation Forest

Assumptions 3 conditions, and the second one is built into the cuts.

AssumptionWhat happens when it fails
Outliers are few and differentThe name is literal: a large group of outliers stops being easy to isolate, because it cuts like a cluster.
Cuts parallel to the axes are enoughEvery cut is vertical or horizontal. An outlier that is only unusual along a diagonal needs many cuts.
You know roughly how many to flagThe score is a ranking. The contamination setting, or a count you pick, decides where the list stops.
Isolation Forest

Drawbacks On checkup the top 14 scores catch 4 of the 5 joint rows. Row 33 lies off the trend along a diagonal, where axis cuts are slow.

checkup, the 14 highest scores ringed

Axis-parallel bias

The heat map on the mechanism slide rises in horizontal and vertical bands, not in rings. Extended Isolation Forest, 2018, cuts at random angles.

A ranking without a cutoff

Top 14 caught 4 of 5 joint rows and flagged 8 clean ones. The count was a choice.

Randomness

Scores move between runs. Fix the seed, and use enough trees that the ranking stops changing.

One-Class SVM

Concept Learn a boundary that encloses most of the data, and call whatever falls outside it an outlier.

boundary at ν = 0.05, γ = 0.5 on standardised shops

Schölkopf et al., 2001

Map the rows through a kernel, then find the boundary that separates them from the origin with the widest margin.

The RBF kernel

Similarity falls off with distance at rate γ. Small γ gives a smooth blob; large γ wraps each small group separately.

It is a classifier trained with one class. Everything it sees in training is treated as normal.
One-Class SVM

Example With ν = 0.05 it flags 16 rows: 1 of 4 local, both global, 5 kiosks and 8 supermarkets.

the rows outside the boundary, by what was planted
plantedflagged
local1 of 4
global2 of 2
kiosk5 of 150
supermarket8 of 150

Three local rows missed

At this γ the boundary is drawn around the kiosks generously enough to take in the rows beside them.

The count was set in advance

ν = 0.05 of 306 rows is 15.3. The method flagged 16, close to what it was told.

One-Class SVM

Mechanism Two settings drive it: ν bounds the share of rows left outside, γ sets how tightly the boundary follows the data.

the same ν = 0.05 at three values of γ
k(x, y) = exp( −γ ‖x − y‖² ) ν ≥ share of rows outside the boundary ν ≤ share of rows that are support vectors
γflaggedlocal caught
0.1160 of 4
0.5161 of 4
5162 of 4
All three runs flag 16 rows. γ moves which rows; ν fixed how many.
One-Class SVM

Assumptions 3 conditions, two of them about settings you cannot learn from unlabelled data.

AssumptionWhat happens when it fails
Outliers are a small share of the training rowsOutliers in training pull the boundary out toward themselves. ν is the only allowance for them.
γ matches the scale of the structureOne γ serves the whole plane. Two formats with different spreads need two.
Columns are scaledThe kernel uses Euclidean distance, so an unscaled column dominates exactly as in LOF.
One-Class SVM

Drawbacks ν decides how many rows are flagged and γ decides which. Neither can be tuned without labels.

the three boundaries again

One γ for two densities

At γ = 0.1 it catches 0 of 4 local rows. At γ = 5 it catches 2 and flags 11 supermarkets as it wraps them in pieces.

ν is a quota

ν × n = 15.3 here, and every γ returned 16. The count does not depend on how many outliers the file holds.

Where it fits

Novelty detection: train on data known to be clean, then score new rows. For cleaning a single file, LOF or Isolation Forest need fewer guesses.

DBSCAN

Concept Grow clusters from rows with enough close neighbours. Rows that no cluster reaches are noise, and noise is the outlier list.

DBSCAN at eps = 0.3, minPts = 5: clusters outlined, noise filled red

Ester, Kriegel, Sander and Xu, 1996

A clustering method. Outliers fall out as the rows it declines to cluster.

row typerule
coreat least minPts rows within eps
borderwithin eps of a core row
noiseneither
No cluster count to set. The data decides how many clusters there are.
DBSCAN · step 1 of 5

Intuition Draw a circle of radius eps around a row and count the rows inside it, the row itself included. On standardised shops at eps = 0.3, a kiosk counts 152.

standardised shops, equal scales on both axes
N(p) = rows within eps of p, p included
rowrows in its circle
kiosk, row 1152
supermarket, row 14233
global, row 1391
The count is a density: rows per circle of a fixed size. One kiosk's circle holds every kiosk and local rows 72 and 76.
DBSCAN · step 2 of 5

Intuition continued 1 A row whose circle holds at least minPts = 5 rows is a core row. 293 of the 306 rows are core.

core rows filled, eps = 0.3
core: N(p) ≥ minPts = 5

3 of the 4 local rows are core rows themselves. Their circles reach into the kiosk cluster and fill up with kiosks.
DBSCAN · step 3 of 5

Intuition continued 2 A row that misses the core count but sits inside a core row’s circle is a border row. 9 rows are border rows here.

Row 7

Its own circle holds 3 rows, short of 5. It sits 0.144 from row 245, a core row, so it is a border row.

A border row joins a cluster but cannot extend it: its circle is too sparse to recruit further rows.
DBSCAN · step 4 of 5

Intuition continued 3 Core rows inside each other’s circles chain into one cluster. Shops gives 2 chains, and the 4 rows no chain reaches are noise.

one spanning tree of core links per cluster, eps = 0.3
1. link core rows within eps of each other 2. each connected chain is a cluster 3. border rows join the chain that reaches them 4. rows no chain reaches are noise
labelrows
cluster 1154: 150 kiosk, 4 local
cluster 2148 supermarket
noise4: 2 global, 2 supermarket
The chains set the number of clusters. Noise is what is left over, and noise is the outlier list.
DBSCAN · step 5 of 5

Intuition continued 4 The core test is a k-distance test: a row is core when its 4th-nearest neighbour lies within eps, one cutoff for both formats.

distance to the 4th-nearest neighbour, by planted group
core ⇔ 4th-neighbour distance ≤ eps (minPts = 5 counts the row itself)

Reached, so not noise

Rows 72, 76 and 245 are core rows, their circles filled by kiosks. Row 7 is a border row inside row 245’s circle. All four join the kiosk cluster.

DBSCAN

Mechanism Sort every row's distance to its (minPts − 1)-th neighbour; the bend in that curve suggests eps.

sorted 4th-neighbour distances on standardised shops
1. pick an unvisited core row, start a cluster 2. add every row within eps of it 3. repeat from each new core row 4. rows never added are noise

Two shoulders

The kiosks need a tiny eps and the supermarkets a large one. The curve has no single bend.

Rule of thumb: minPts ≥ p + 1, and 2p for noisy data. Here p = 2 and minPts = 5.
DBSCAN

Assumptions 2 conditions, and shops breaks the first.

AssumptionWhat happens when it fails
Clusters share one densityOne eps defines dense for the whole file. A tight format and a loose one cannot both be dense at the same eps.
eps and minPts are meaningful after scalingeps is a distance in the standardised space. Change the scaling and the right eps changes with it.
DBSCAN

Drawbacks No single eps finds the local rows without calling a large share of supermarkets noise. Drag it and check.

eps0.30
minPts = 5 throughout. Labels computed with sklearn on the standardised columns.
noiserows

The trade

At eps 0.05 all 4 local rows are noise, and so are 144 supermarkets. By 0.20 every local row has joined the kiosks.

Treatment

Concept Detection gives a list of rows. What to do with each one depends on why it is there, which is the cause column from lecture 4.

from a flagged row to an action

Diagnose first

Open the row. Check its source, its neighbours in time, the other columns of the same record.

Errors with a known fix

The decimal slips and pound entries: correct them. The information comes back.

Errors without one

The joint rows: the true weight is unknown, so the value becomes a missing value and lectures 1 to 3 take over.

Real values

The 138.0 kg adult and the Blue Metal jump stay. The model changes instead of the data.

Treatment

Mechanism What each action does to a flagged value, and what has to be true for it to be right.

actionwhat it doesright when
correctreplaces it with the true valuethe cause is known and reversible
set to missingremoves the value, keeps the rowthe value is wrong and the rest of the row is fine
delete the rowremoves everything in the rowthe flagged rows are a random subset: MCAR, from lecture 1
winsorisemoves it to a percentilethe value is real and only its leverage is a problem
cap at a fencemoves it to the IQR fencesame as winsorising, with the fence as the limit
transformlog or square root of the columnthe column is skewed and the extreme values are real
keep, robust modelleaves it; the fit down-weights ityou trust the value more than your diagnosis
Treatment

Example Regress weight on height in checkup. The clean-row slope is 0.779; the raw file gives 0.525, and each treatment lands somewhere between.

fitted slope under each treatment of the raw file

clean rows only0.77971.0311.00

Deleting and correcting the 7 errors give the same slope. The difference is 7 rows of height data kept.
The joint rows still pull the slope from 0.764 to 0.685 after the errors are fixed.
Treatment

Example continued 1 Leave every error in and fit a Huber regression instead. The slope is 0.744, closer to the clean rows than any cleaning except the last.

the same comparison with the robust fit added

Huber regression

Squared loss for small residuals, absolute loss past a threshold. A 700 kg row pulls on the line with a constant force instead of a squared one.

ordinary least squares, raw 0.525 Huber, raw 0.744 correct errors, drop joint 0.764 clean rows only 0.779
Robust fitting is a treatment too, and a good default when the diagnosis is uncertain. It does not repair the file for the next analyst.
Treatment

Assumptions Each action rests on a claim about the flagged rows, and deletion rests on the one lecture 1 warned about.

AssumptionWhat happens when it fails
Deletion: the flagged rows are MCARIf the pound entries all came from one clinic, deleting them deletes that clinic's patients. That is deletion under MAR, and it biases every mean by clinic.
Winsorising: the extreme values are realIt assumes the value is right and only too influential. On an error it keeps a wrong value, just a smaller one.
Transform: the skew is the population'sA log on weight shrinks 701 to 6.55, still the largest value in the column, and still an error.
Correction: the cause is certainDividing by 10 is right for a decimal slip and wrong for a 700 kg reading that is a different error.
Treatment

Drawbacks Winsorising the raw file at the 1st and 99th percentiles clips at 159.1 kg. The three decimal slips become three 159.1 kg adults.

what winsorising writes into the file

342701159.170.1
The slope after winsorising is 0.661, the worst of the cleaning treatments.

It hides the error

The next person sees a heavy adult, not a typo. Nothing in the column says a value was changed.

It hides real events

Lecture 4: capping the Blue Metal jump leaves every later price 20.7% too low.

Any change to a value goes in the cleaning log, with the rows it touched and the cause it assumed.

Before Lecture 6

Practice Three exercises on the two files.

  1. Run Mahalanobis distance on shops once per format, splitting on floor area at 150 sqm. Report which rows each run flags.
  2. Run LOF on shops without standardising. Explain which column now decides the neighbours, and what happens to rows 7 and 245.
  3. Set the 5 joint weights in checkup to missing and impute them by regression on height, as in lecture 3. Refit the slope and compare it with 0.779.
